title: Simplified insecticide toxicity determination method for Nesidiocoris tenuis using contaminated diet
author: Wari, Takagi, et al.

steps.title: Prepare containment tube
steps.instruction: Take a 50 mL Falcon tube, drill two holes on the bottom side sized for 1000 µL pipette tips, insert the pipette tip ends and secure each with a 0.1 µm mass to allow ventilation without suffocating the insects; invert the tube so the lid becomes the base, trim a filter paper to fit inside the lid and place it there.

steps.title: Hatch and sterilize brine shrimp eggs
steps.instruction: Weigh 0.05–0.08 g Artemia eggs into a 15 mL Falcon tube, add 10 mL of 25 ppt NaCl solution whose pH is adjusted to 8.0 with MgSO₄, drill a hole in the tube lid and fasten it, incubate at 26–28 °C with a 16 h light : 8 h dark cycle for 16–24 h, then decant the liquid and keep the hatched eggs; verify hatching under a light microscope and sterilize the eggs in a clean bench under UV light for at least 1 h.

steps.title: Prepare host plant leaves
steps.instruction: Cut leaves from a host plant of N. tenuis to roughly 40 mm diameter so they will sit flat on the filter paper placed inside the tube lid.

steps.title: Make pesticide solution
steps.instruction: In a 200 mL beaker, prepare the pesticide solution at the desired concentration for the assay; this volume is sufficient to dip both the leaves and the hatched brine shrimp eggs.

steps.title: Dip leaves in pesticide
steps.instruction: Submerge each prepared leaf in the pesticide solution for exactly 25 seconds, then remove and allow to air‑dry for 60–90 minutes.

steps.title: Dip brine shrimp eggs in pesticide
steps.instruction: After UV sterilization, dip the hatched brine shrimp eggs into the same pesticide solution for 25 seconds and air‑dry for 60–90 minutes.

steps.title: Assemble contaminated diet in tube
steps.instruction: Place the air‑dried, pesticide‑treated leaves onto the filter paper inside the tube lid, then distribute the air‑dried, pesticide‑contaminated brine shrimp eggs onto the leaves.

steps.title: Introduce N. tenuis specimens
steps.instruction: Add 15–20 N. tenuis individuals (either all nymphs or all adults) into the containment tube containing the contaminated diet.

steps.title: Incubate assay containers
steps.instruction: Put the sealed containment tubes in an incubator set to 25 ± 1 °C, 65 ± 10 % relative humidity, with a 16 h light : 8 h dark photoperiod for 72 hours.

steps.title: Assess mortality after 72 h
steps.instruction: After 72 hours, gently touch each insect with a brush; individuals that show no movement are recorded as dead.

steps.title: Calculate corrected mortality
steps.instruction: Compute corrected mortality using Abbott’s formula or the simplified equation: Corrected Mortality (%) = [(control – test)/control] × 100 %.

description: Bemisia tabaci is a notorious pest for major vegetable crops and until recently, B. tabaci management has been mostly relied upon insecticides as the primary control approach. Augmenting Biological Control Agents (BCAs); i.e. parasitoids, predators and microbial entomopathogenic fungi into the chemical control system offers a key strategy, whose potential have been realized however lacking comprehensive studies in open and/or protected cropping systems. To minimize the overuse of insecticides, augmenting N. tenuis has been promoted and recommended to be assimilated into B. tabaci Integrated Pest Management (IPM) system. However, to use both insecticides and N. tenuis in the B. tabaci IPM system, highly toxic insecticides must be avoided as much as possible in-order for the biological control agents such as N. tenuis to work efficiently. To determine insecticides that are toxic to B. tabaci but less toxic to N. tenuis, we developed a bioassay method using contaminated brine shrimp eggs as well as contaminated leaves to mimic N. tenuis feeding on live specimens of B. tabaci nymphs and tomato plants when sprayed upon with an insecticide. Using four insecticides registered for B. tabaci control in tomato production in Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan as representatives from insecticides use in B. tabaci control, bioassays were performed on nymphs and adults of B. tabaci and N. tenuis. Here, we show that this method, while simulating actual field situations, we used insecticide contaminated brine shrimp eggs to pre-determine the compatibility and incompatibility of insecticides against N. tenuis nymphs and adults. Bioassay results revealed that dinotefuran, was toxic to both B. tabaci and N. tenuis nymphs and adults with more than 80% mortality (Table 1), suggesting that neonicotinoids are harmful and may not be compatible for use with N. tenuis in field conditions.
